section: Authoring Documents with R Markdown and Generating PDF Output
text:
Authoring Documents with R Markdown and Generating PDF Output
R Markdown is a document format that integrates prose, code, and computational output within a single reproducible file. The following steps outline the process of creating an R Markdown document and rendering it as a PDF.

Step 1: Install Required Packages
Execute the following commands in the RStudio Console:
install.packages("rmarkdown")
install.packages("knitr")


Step 2: Install a LaTeX Distribution
PDF rendering requires a LaTeX engine. The tinytex package provides a lightweight, self-contained LaTeX distribution suitable for most use cases:
install.packages("tinytex")
tinytex::install_tinytex()
Restart RStudio after installation to ensure the LaTeX binaries are correctly registered.


Step 3: Create a New R Markdown File

From the RStudio menu, select: File → New File → R Markdown…
Specify a title and author in the dialogue box; set the default output format to PDF
Click OK to generate the template file



Step 4: Configure the YAML Header
Every R Markdown document begins with a YAML front matter block delimited by ---. This block controls document metadata and output settings:
---
title: "Assignment Title"
author: "Full Name (Student ID)"
date: "2024-01-01"
output: pdf_document
---


Step 5: Write Document Content
R Markdown uses standard Markdown syntax for formatting prose, supplemented by fenced code chunks for embedding R code:



Syntax
Rendered Output




# Heading 1
First-level heading


## Heading 2
Second-level heading


**bold**
bold


*italic*
italic


Fenced code block with {r}
Executed R code with output



Example code chunk:

```{r}
summary(mtcars)
```

Each course follows the same structure: a lecture hour for conceptual foundations and a lab hour for hands-on in-class exercises.

text:
Instructions

Structural & Stylistic Alignment Replicate the exact formatting, structural hierarchy, and stylistic layout of the provided slides (found in the ch2 directory) to ensure visual and pedagogical consistency across all chapters.
Comprehensive Mathematical Examples & R Integration Ensure that all content from the source text, including every example, is thoroughly extracted and incorporated into the output. Each example must be accompanied by a comprehensive, step-by-step solution implemented in R. The final output must explicitly present both the clean R code and its corresponding execution results, mirroring the format of the referenced slides.
Paraphrasing & Academic Integrity To prevent plagiarism, you must completely rewrite and paraphrase all textual descriptions, definitions, explanations, and commentary from the textbook. The narrative flow, tone, and wording must be entirely original, rigorous yet accessible, and tailored specifically for a student audience, while strictly preserving the technical and mathematical accuracy of the original content.
Strategic Use of Callout Blocks Utilize visually distinct callout blocks (e.g., alert/info/note boxes) to segment key information and enhance readability. Specifically, apply callout blocks in the following scenarios:

Definitions & Formulas: Whenever the textbook presents a standard definition box or a key mathematical formula.
Example Prompts: Enclose the initial question/prompt of every example within a callout block to separate it clearly from its solution and R code.

Directory and Storage Architecture Replicate the established file structure utilized in the previous modules. Dynamically generate and store the output within the newly designated directory (e.g., ch3/), precisely mirroring the organization, sub-folders, and naming conventions of the repository.

title: Statistics
section: From Raw Data to Organized Information
text:
From Raw Data to Organized Information
When data are first gathered, they exist in raw form — an unordered, unprocessed list of values. On their own, raw data reveal very little about the underlying patterns or trends in a dataset.
Organizing data into a frequency distribution provides a structured summary that makes patterns visible and analysis manageable.






Frequency Distribution


A frequency distribution is a table that organizes data values (or ranges of values) along with the count of how often each value or range occurs in the dataset.

title: Statistics
text:
Categorical Frequency Distributions
When data consist of qualitative categories (non-numeric labels or groups), a categorical frequency distribution is used. Each category is listed alongside its frequency and relative frequency (percentage).
Steps to construct a categorical frequency distribution:

List each distinct category.
Tally the occurrences of each category.
Record the frequency and compute the percentage: \% = \frac{f}{n} \times 100

title: Statistics
section: Example 2-1: Blood Types of Army Inductees
text:
Example 2-1: Blood Types of Army Inductees






Example 2-1


A sample of 25 army inductees was tested for blood type. The results are shown below. Organize the data into a categorical frequency distribution.

O  O  B  AB  B
B  B  O  A   O
A  O  O  O   AB
AB A  O  B   A

title: Statistics
text:
Example 2-1: Solution

blood <- c("A","B","B","AB","O","O","O","B","AB","B",
           "B","B","O","A","O","A","O","O","O","AB",
           "AB","A","O","B","A")

df <- data.frame(blood) |>
  count(blood) |>
  rename(Class = blood, Frequency = n) |>
  mutate(Percentage = round(Frequency / sum(Frequency) * 100, 1))

title: Statistics

Example 2-1: Interpretation
The frequency distribution reveals that Type O is the most common blood type in this sample, occurring 9 times (36%). Type A appears 5 times (20%), Type B appears 6 times (24%), and Type AB appears 4 times (16%).

ggplot(df, aes(x = reorder(Class, -Frequency), y = Frequency, fill = Class)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = Frequency), vjust = -0.3) +
  labs(title = "Blood Types of 25 Army Inductees",
       x = "Blood Type", y = "Frequency") +
  theme_minimal()

title: Statistics
text:
Grouped Frequency Distributions
When dealing with quantitative data that span a wide range of values, individual values are grouped into classes (intervals). The resulting table is called a grouped frequency distribution.
Key terminology:

Class limits: The smallest (lower) and largest (upper) values that can belong to a class.
Class boundaries: Values halfway between the upper limit of one class and the lower limit of the next, eliminating gaps.
Class width: The difference between consecutive lower class limits (or upper class boundaries).
Class midpoint: X_m = \dfrac{\text{lower limit} + \text{upper limit}}{2}

title: Statistics
section: Rules for Constructing a Grouped Frequency Distribution
text:
Rules for Constructing a Grouped Frequency Distribution






Six Construction Guidelines



Use between 5 and 20 classes — enough to show pattern without excessive detail.
The class width should be an odd number when possible so midpoints are whole numbers.
Classes must be mutually exclusive — each data value belongs to exactly one class.
Classes must be continuous — no gaps between classes, even if some classes have zero frequency.
Classes must be exhaustive — every data value must fit into some class.
Classes should be equal in width (except possibly the first or last class).

Formula: \text{Class width} \approx \dfrac{\text{highest value} - \text{lowest value}}{\text{number of classes}}

text:
Example 2-2: Record High Temperatures

110 118 117 116 118 122 114 114 105 109
107 112 114 115 118 117 118 122 106 110

120 113 120 117 105 110 118 112 114 114

title: Statistics
text:
Example 2-2: Visualization

ggplot(data.frame(temps), aes(x = temps)) +
  geom_histogram(breaks = breaks, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(100, 135, by = 5)) +
  labs(title = "Record High Temperatures for 50 U.S. States",
       x = "Temperature (°F)", y = "Frequency") +
  theme_minimal()

title: Statistics
text:
Ungrouped Frequency Distributions
When the range of values is small and each distinct value is meaningful on its own, an ungrouped (single-value) frequency distribution lists each individual data value as its own class.
This approach preserves the exact values rather than collapsing them into intervals.

section: Example 2-3: Miles per Gallon for SUVs
text:
Example 2-3: Miles per Gallon for SUVs






Example 2-3


The fuel economy ratings (mpg) for a sample of 30 sport utility vehicles are listed below. Construct an ungrouped frequency distribution.
12 17 12 14 16 18 16 18 12 16
15 15 16 12 15 15 16 16 12 14
15 12 15 15 12 16 15 16 16 12

title: Statistics
Statistics
text:
Cumulative Frequency Distributions
A cumulative frequency distribution shows the running total of frequencies from the lowest class up through each successive class. It answers the question: “How many observations fall at or below this value?”

title: Statistics
text:
Graphing Grouped Frequency Distributions
Three fundamental graphs are used to visualize data organized in a grouped frequency distribution:

Histogram — bars whose heights represent frequencies (or relative frequencies), with no gaps between bars.
Frequency polygon — a line graph connecting the midpoints of each class at their frequency values; extended to the x-axis at each end.
Ogive (oh-jive) — a cumulative frequency graph; shows the running total of observations up to each class boundary.

title: Statistics
text:
The Histogram






Histogram


A histogram is a bar graph in which the horizontal axis represents the class boundaries and the vertical axis represents the frequencies (or relative frequencies). Adjacent bars share boundaries — there are no gaps.

title: Statistics
section: Example 2-4: Histogram of Record High Temperatures
text:
Example 2-4: Histogram of Record High Temperatures






Example 2-4


Using the frequency distribution from Example 2-2, draw a histogram for the record high temperatures of the 50 U.S. states.

title: Statistics
text:
The Frequency Polygon






Frequency Polygon


A frequency polygon is a line graph drawn by connecting the midpoints of the tops of each histogram bar. The line is extended to the x-axis one class width beyond each end, so the polygon is “closed.”

title: Statistics
text:
Example 2-5: Frequency Polygon






Example 2-5


Draw a frequency polygon for the record high temperatures data from Example 2-2.

title: Statistics
text:
The Ogive






Ogive


An ogive (cumulative frequency graph) plots the upper class boundaries on the x-axis against the cumulative frequencies on the y-axis. It is useful for determining how many observations fall below a particular value.

title: Statistics
section: Example 2-6: Ogive for Record High Temperatures
text:
Example 2-6: Ogive for Record High Temperatures






Example 2-6


Draw an ogive for the record high temperatures distribution from Example 2-2.

title: Statistics
text:
Relative Frequency Graphs
All three graph types (histogram, frequency polygon, ogive) can be redrawn using relative frequencies (proportions or percentages) instead of raw counts. The shape of the graph is identical, but the vertical axis reflects the fraction of total observations rather than the count.
Relative frequency graphs facilitate comparisons between datasets of different sizes.

Distribution Shapes
The overall shape of a distribution describes how data values are spread across the range. Recognizing shape helps in choosing appropriate statistical methods.

title: Statistics
text:
Visualizing Distribution Shapes

set.seed(42)

make_hist <- function(data, title, fill_col) {
  ggplot(data.frame(x = data), aes(x)) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = fill_col, color = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
    labs(title = title, x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
    theme(axis.text = element_blank())
}

p_bell    <- make_hist(rnorm(500, 50, 10),     "Bell-shaped",    "#4a90d9")
p_uni     <- make_hist(runif(500, 20, 80),     "Uniform",        "#f0ad4e")
p_right   <- make_hist(rexp(500, 0.05),        "Right-skewed",   "#d9534f")
p_left    <- make_hist(80 - rexp(500, 0.05),   "Left-skewed",    "#5cb85c")
p_bimod   <- make_hist(c(rnorm(250,30,5), rnorm(250,70,5)), "Bimodal", "#9b59b6")
p_u       <- make_hist(c(rnorm(200,20,5), rnorm(200,80,5)), "U-shaped", "#1abc9c")

title: Statistics
text:
Beyond the Histogram
In addition to histograms, frequency polygons, and ogives, several other graphical tools are widely used in statistics and everyday data communication:

Bar graphs — for comparing frequencies of categorical data
Pareto charts — bar graphs with bars sorted from highest to lowest frequency
Time series graphs — for tracking a variable’s change over time
Pie graphs — for showing each category’s share of the whole
Stem and leaf plots — for displaying the actual data values in a graphical form

title: Statistics
text:
Bar Graphs






Bar Graph


A bar graph represents categorical (qualitative) data using horizontal or vertical bars. The length or height of each bar corresponds to the frequency or value for that category. Unlike a histogram, gaps between bars are acceptable.

title: Statistics
text:
Pareto Charts






Pareto Chart


A Pareto chart is a specialized bar graph in which the categories are arranged in descending order of frequency. It is particularly useful for identifying which categories account for the largest share of the total — a key concept in quality control and decision-making.



The name honors Vilfredo Pareto, who observed that a small number of causes often account for the majority of effects (the “80/20 rule”).

title: Statistics
text:
Pie Graphs






Pie Graph


A pie graph (pie chart) is a circle divided into sectors, where each sector represents a category. The size of each sector is proportional to that category’s share of the total.
Formula for sector angle: \text{Degrees} = \frac{f}{n} \times 360°
where f is the category frequency and n is the total number of observations.

title: Statistics
text:
Misleading Graphs






Caution: Graphs Can Mislead


Graphs are powerful communication tools, but they can distort perception. Common misleading techniques include:

Truncating the y-axis — starting the vertical axis at a value other than zero exaggerates differences between bars or points.
Using two-dimensional images for one-dimensional changes — the eye compares areas rather than heights, making small differences appear dramatic.
Omitting axis labels or units — without a labeled y-axis, there is no way to gauge the actual magnitude of differences.

Always examine the scale and labels carefully before drawing conclusions from a graph.

title: Statistics
text:
Stem and Leaf Plots






Stem and Leaf Plot


A stem and leaf plot (stemplot) organizes data by splitting each value into a stem (the leading digit(s)) and a leaf (the trailing digit). This technique preserves the actual data values while displaying them in a graphical form that reveals the shape of the distribution.

Each row represents one stem (class).
Leaves within each row are arranged in ascending order.
The plot functions like a histogram turned on its side.

title: Statistics
section: What Is a Measure of Central Tendency?
text:
What Is a Measure of Central Tendency?
A measure of central tendency is a single numerical value that summarizes the center or “typical” value of a dataset. Rather than examining every individual observation, a central tendency statistic provides a concise snapshot of where data tend to cluster.
The four most widely used measures are:

Mean — arithmetic average of all values
Median — middle value when data are ordered
Mode — most frequently occurring value(s)
Midrange — midpoint between the highest and lowest values

title: Statistics
text:
The Mean
The mean is computed by summing all data values and dividing by the number of observations. It is the most commonly reported measure of center.






Formulas for the Mean


Sample mean: \bar{X} = \frac{\Sigma X}{n}
Population mean: \mu = \frac{\Sigma X}{N}
where \Sigma X is the sum of all data values and n (or N) is the count of values.









Rounding Rule


Round the mean to one more decimal place than appears in the original data.

title: Statistics
text:
Mean for Grouped Data
When raw data are unavailable and only a frequency distribution is given, use the midpoint of each class to approximate the mean.






Formula — Mean for Grouped Data


\bar{X} = \frac{\Sigma f \cdot X_m}{n}
where f = class frequency, X_m = class midpoint, n = \Sigma f.

title: Statistics
text:
The Median
The median is the value that sits at the exact center of an ordered dataset, dividing it into two equal halves. It is resistant to the influence of extreme values.






Finding the Median



Arrange all data values from lowest to highest.
If n is odd: the median is the middle value — position \frac{n+1}{2}.
If n is even: the median is the average of the two middle values.

rooms <- c(713, 300, 618, 595, 311, 401, 292)
sorted <- sort(rooms)
cat("Sorted:", sorted, "\n")

Sorted: 292 300 311 401 595 618 713 

cat("Median position:", (length(rooms)+1)/2, "\n")

Median position: 4 

cat("Median:", median(rooms), "\n")

Median: 401 


With 7 values (odd), the median is the 4th value when sorted: 401 rooms.

Sorted: 3 5 8 10 12 14 15 25

    length(fees)/2, "and", length(fees)/2 + 1, "\n")

title: Statistics
text:
The Mode
The mode is the value that appears most frequently in a dataset. Unlike the mean and median, the mode can be used with both quantitative and qualitative data.






Key Properties of the Mode



A dataset may have no mode (all values appear once), one mode (unimodal), two modes (bimodal), or more (multimodal).
For grouped data, the modal class is the class with the highest frequency.
Mode is the only appropriate measure of center for nominal (categorical) data.

The Midrange
The midrange is the arithmetic mean of the maximum and minimum data values. It is easy to calculate but highly sensitive to extreme values.

The Weighted Mean

section: Choosing the Right Measure of Center
text:
Choosing the Right Measure of Center






Which Measure to Use?





Situation
Best Measure




Most typical value desired
Mode


Distribution is open-ended (no max/min)
Median


Extreme values are present
Median


Data are categorical (nominal)
Mode


Further computations are needed
Mean


Data must be split into two equal groups
Median



The mean is generally preferred when data are approximately symmetric with no extreme outliers, since it uses every data value in its computation.

title: Statistics
text:
Why Variation Matters
Two datasets can have identical means yet differ dramatically in their spread. Measures of variation quantify how spread out or clustered data values are around the center.






Three Key Measures of Variation





Measure
Symbol(s)
Description




Range
R
Distance between highest and lowest


Variance
\sigma^2, s^2
Average squared distance from mean


Standard Deviation
\sigma, s
Square root of variance

section: Example 3-18: Why the Mean Alone Is Insufficient
text:
Example 3-18: Why the Mean Alone Is Insufficient






Example 3-18


A testing laboratory evaluates two brands of outdoor paint to see how long (in months) each lasts before fading. Six cans of each brand were tested.
Brand A: 10, 60, 50, 30, 40, 20 — Mean = 35 months Brand B: 35, 45, 30, 35, 40, 25 — Mean = 35 months




A <- c(10, 60, 50, 30, 40, 20)
B <- c(35, 45, 30, 35, 40, 25)
cat("Brand A mean:", mean(A), "| Brand B mean:", mean(B), "\n")

title: Statistics
text:
The Range
The range is the simplest measure of spread — the difference between the largest and smallest values.






Formula — Range


R = \text{highest value} - \text{lowest value}









Limitation of the Range


A single extreme value can drastically inflate the range, making it a misleading indicator of typical variation.

title: Statistics
text:
Population Variance and Standard Deviation
The variance measures the average squared deviation of each value from the mean. The standard deviation is its square root, expressed in the original units.






Population Formulas


\sigma^2 = \frac{\Sigma(X - \mu)^2}{N} \qquad \sigma = \sqrt{\frac{\Sigma(X - \mu)^2}{N}}
Step-by-step procedure:

Find the population mean \mu.
Subtract \mu from each value: (X - \mu).
Square each difference: (X - \mu)^2.
Sum all squared differences.
Divide by N to get variance; take the square root for \sigma.

text:
Coefficient of Variation
The coefficient of variation (CVar) expresses the standard deviation as a percentage of the mean, enabling comparison of variability across datasets with different units or different scales.






Formula — Coefficient of Variation


\text{CVar} = \frac{s}{\bar{X}} \times 100\% \quad \text{(samples)} \qquad \text{CVar} = \frac{\sigma}{\mu} \times 100\% \quad \text{(populations)}

title: Statistics
text:
Range Rule of Thumb
The range rule of thumb provides a quick approximation of the standard deviation using only the range.






Range Rule of Thumb


s \approx \frac{\text{range}}{4}
Conversely, most data values fall within the interval: [\bar{X} - 2s, \; \bar{X} + 2s]



This approximation works best for unimodal, roughly symmetric distributions.

title: Statistics
text:
Chebyshev’s Theorem
Chebyshev’s theorem provides a guaranteed lower bound on the proportion of data values that fall within k standard deviations of the mean — regardless of the distribution’s shape.






Chebyshev’s Theorem


The proportion of values from any data set that will fall within k standard deviations of the mean is at least:
1 - \frac{1}{k^2}, \quad k > 1



k
Minimum % within k SDs




2
At least 75%


3
At least 88.89%


2.5
At least 84%

title: Statistics
text:
Example 3-27: Home Prices (Chebyshev)






Example 3-27


The mean price of homes in a neighborhood is $50,000 and the standard deviation is $10,000. Find the price range in which at least 75% of homes will sell.




mu  <- 50000
sd  <- 10000
k   <- 2   # gives at least 75%

lower <- mu - k * sd
upper <- mu + k * sd
pct   <- (1 - 1/k^2) * 100

cat("k =", k, "→ at least", pct, "% of values\n")

k = 2 → at least 75 % of values

cat("Price range: $", lower, "to $", upper, "\n")

Price range: $ 30000 to $ 70000 


At least 75% of homes will sell between $30,000 and $70,000.

The Empirical (Normal) Rule
When a distribution is bell-shaped (normal), tighter guarantees apply:






The Empirical Rule


For bell-shaped distributions:



Interval

title: Statistics
section: Locating a Value Within a Distribution
text:
Locating a Value Within a Distribution
Measures of position describe where a particular value stands in relation to the rest of the dataset. They answer the question: How does this value compare to others?
Key position measures include:

Standard score (z-score) — distance from mean in standard deviation units
Percentiles — divide data into 100 equal groups
Deciles — divide data into 10 equal groups
Quartiles — divide data into 4 equal groups

title: Statistics
text:
Standard Scores (z-Scores)
A z-score (standard score) converts a raw value into the number of standard deviations it lies above or below the mean, enabling fair comparison across different distributions.






z-Score Formulas


z = \frac{X - \bar{X}}{s} \quad \text{(sample)} \qquad z = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma} \quad \text{(population)}

z > 0: value is above the mean
z = 0: value equals the mean
z < 0: value is below the mean

title: Statistics
text:
Example 3-29: Comparing Test Performance






Example 3-29


A student scored 65 on a calculus exam (\bar{X}=50, s=10) and 30 on a history exam (\bar{X}=25, s=5). On which test did she perform relatively better?




z_calc <- (65 - 50) / 10
z_hist <- (30 - 25) / 5

cat("Calculus z-score:", z_calc, "\n")

Calculus z-score: 1.5 

cat("History z-score:", z_hist, "\n")

History z-score: 1 

cat("\nBoth z-scores are equal (1.5) → same relative performance.\n")


Both z-scores are equal (1.5) → same relative performance.


Both scores are 1.5 standard deviations above their respective means — equal relative positions.

title: Statistics
text:
Percentiles
Percentiles locate a data value’s position in hundredths. A value at the pth percentile exceeds p% of all values in the distribution.






Percentile Formula


\text{Percentile rank of } X = \frac{(\text{number of values below } X) + 0.5}{\text{total number of values}} \times 100
To find the value corresponding to a given percentile p:
c = \frac{n \cdot p}{100}

If c is not a whole number: round up and use that position.
If c is a whole number: average the cth and (c+1)th values.

title: Statistics
text:
Quartiles and Deciles
Quartiles divide the dataset into four equal groups (Q_1, Q_2, Q_3), while deciles divide it into ten groups (D_1, \ldots, D_9).






Key Relationships





Position Measure
Percentile Equivalent




Q_1 (1st quartile)
P_{25}


Q_2 (2nd quartile = median)
P_{50}


Q_3 (3rd quartile)
P_{75}


D_1 (1st decile)
P_{10}


D_5 (5th decile)
P_{50}



Interquartile Range (IQR): \text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1
The IQR measures the spread of the middle 50% of the data.

title: Statistics
text:
Finding Quartiles — Procedure






Step-by-Step Procedure for Q1, Q2, Q3



Arrange data from lowest to highest.
Find the median (Q_2) of the entire dataset.
Find the median of the lower half (below Q_2) → this is Q_1.
Find the median of the upper half (above Q_2) → this is Q_3.

title: Statistics
text:
Example 3-36: Finding Quartiles






Example 3-36


Find Q_1, Q_2, and Q_3 for the data set: 15, 13, 6, 5, 12, 50, 22, 18

xs <- sort(x)
cat("Sorted data:", xs, "\n\n")

title: Statistics
text:
Outliers
An outlier is an extremely high or low data value that stands apart from the rest of the distribution. Outliers can distort the mean and standard deviation significantly.






Procedure for Identifying Outliers



Arrange data and find Q_1 and Q_3.
Compute \text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1.
Multiply: 1.5 \times \text{IQR}.
Compute fences: lower fence = Q_1 - 1.5(\text{IQR}); upper fence = Q_3 + 1.5(\text{IQR}).
Any value outside these fences is a suspected outlier.

title: Statistics
text:

(This is the sorted version of Example 3-36’s data.)

Q1 <- 9; Q3 <- 20  # from Example 3-36
IQR_val <- Q3 - Q1

lower_fence <- Q1 - 1.5 * IQR_val
upper_fence <- Q3 + 1.5 * IQR_val

title: Statistics
text:
Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
Exploratory data analysis (EDA), introduced by John Tukey, uses graphical and resistant statistics to uncover patterns, distribution shape, and potential outliers without assuming a particular model.






Traditional vs. EDA Approaches





Traditional
Exploratory Data Analysis




Frequency distribution
Stem-and-leaf plot


Histogram
Boxplot


Mean
Median


Standard deviation
Interquartile range (IQR)



EDA statistics (median, IQR) are resistant — less influenced by extreme values — while mean and standard deviation are nonresistant.

title: Statistics
text:
The Five-Number Summary
A five-number summary captures the full spread and shape of a distribution using five key values:






Five-Number Summary



Minimum — lowest data value
Q_1 — first quartile (25th percentile)
Median (Q_2) — middle value (50th percentile)
Q_3 — third quartile (75th percentile)
Maximum — highest data value




These five values form the basis of the boxplot (box-and-whisker plot).

title: Statistics
text:
Constructing a Boxplot






Steps for Building a Boxplot



Find the five-number summary.
Draw a horizontal axis scaled to include the min and max.
Draw a box from Q_1 to Q_3 with a vertical line at the median.
Extend whiskers from the box to the minimum and maximum values.




Reading the Shape from a Boxplot:

Median near center of box → approximately symmetric
Median left of center → positively skewed (right-skewed)
Median right of center → negatively skewed (left-skewed)
Longer right whisker → positively skewed
Longer left whisker → negatively skewed

title: Statistics
text:
Summary: Chapter 3 at a Glance






Section 3-1: Measures of Central Tendency


Mean \bar{X} = \frac{\Sigma X}{n} — uses all values; sensitive to outliers
Median — middle value; resistant to outliers
Mode — most frequent; can be used with categorical data
Midrange = \frac{\min + \max}{2} — easily computed; sensitive to extremes
Weighted Mean = \frac{\Sigma wX}{\Sigma w} — accounts for different weights









Section 3-2: Measures of Variation


Range R = \max - \min
Variance s^2 = \frac{n(\Sigma X^2)-(\Sigma X)^2}{n(n-1)}
Standard Deviation s = \sqrt{s^2}
CVar = \frac{s}{\bar{X}} \times 100\% — compares variability across datasets
Chebyshev’s Theorem — at least 1-\frac{1}{k^2} within k SDs (any distribution)
Empirical Rule — 68/95/99.7% within 1/2/3 SDs (bell-shaped only)

title: Statistics
text:
Summary: Chapter 3 at a Glance (cont.)






Section 3-3: Measures of Position


z-score = \frac{X - \bar{X}}{s} — standard deviations from the mean
Percentile rank = \frac{(\text{# below }X)+0.5}{n} \times 100
Quartiles: Q_1 = P_{25}, Q_2 = P_{50}, Q_3 = P_{75}
IQR = Q_3 - Q_1 — spread of the middle 50%
Outlier fences: Q_1 - 1.5(\text{IQR}) and Q_3 + 1.5(\text{IQR})









Section 3-4: Exploratory Data Analysis


Five-number summary: Min, Q_1, Median, Q_3, Max
Boxplot: visual display of five-number summary revealing center, spread, and skew
EDA statistics (median, IQR) are resistant to outliers
Traditional statistics (mean, SD) are nonresistant

text:
Key Vocabulary







Probability Experiment


A probability experiment is a process that leads to well-defined results called outcomes.











Sample Space and Events



Sample space (S): the set of all possible outcomes of a probability experiment
Outcome: a single result from one trial
Event (E): one or more outcomes — a subset of the sample space
Simple event: an event with exactly one outcome
Compound event: an event with more than one outcome

Classical Probability







Classical Probability


When all outcomes in the sample space are equally likely:
P(E) = \frac{n(E)}{n(S)} = \frac{\text{number of outcomes in event } E}{\text{total outcomes in sample space}}











Probability Rules



0 \leq P(E) \leq 1 for any event E
P(S) = 1 (sum of all outcomes = 1)
P(\emptyset) = 0 (impossible event)
\sum P(E_i) = 1 for all simple events

Mutually Exclusive Events







Mutually Exclusive Events


Two events A and B are mutually exclusive if they cannot occur at the same time — they share no outcomes in common.











Addition Rule 1 — Mutually Exclusive Events


When two events A and B are mutually exclusive: P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B)











Addition Rule 2 — Non-Mutually Exclusive Events


When A and B are not mutually exclusive: P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \text{ and } B)

Three Counting Rules







Three Counting Rules


To determine the total number of possible outcomes:

Fundamental Counting Rule: multiply the number of choices at each step
Permutation Rule: arrangements where order matters
Combination Rule: selections where order does not matter












Fundamental Counting Rule


In a sequence of n events where the first has k_1 possibilities, the second k_2, etc.: \text{Total outcomes} = k_1 \cdot k_2 \cdot k_3 \cdots k_n

title: Statistics
text:
Random Variables






Key Definitions


A random variable is a variable whose value is determined by the outcome of a probability experiment.
A discrete random variable has a finite or countable number of possible values.
A continuous random variable can take on any value in an interval on the number line.



Examples of discrete random variables:

Number of heads in 3 coin tosses: 0, 1, 2, 3
Number of children in a family: 0, 1, 2, 3, …
Number of defects in a batch of products

Examples of continuous random variables:

Height, weight, temperature, time

title: Statistics
text:
Discrete Probability Distributions






Definition


A discrete probability distribution consists of all possible values a discrete random variable can take on, along with their corresponding probabilities.



Two requirements for a valid probability distribution:

The sum of all probabilities must equal 1: \sum P(X) = 1
Each probability must be between 0 and 1: 0 \leq P(X) \leq 1

Probability distributions can be presented as tables, formulas, or graphs.

section: Formulas for Mean, Variance, and Standard Deviation
text:
Formulas for Mean, Variance, and Standard Deviation






Formulas


Mean (Expected Value): \mu = E(X) = \sum X \cdot P(X)
Variance: \sigma^2 = \sum \left[X^2 \cdot P(X)\right] - \mu^2
Standard Deviation: \sigma = \sqrt{\sigma^2}



The mean describes the long-run average outcome of the experiment. The variance and standard deviation measure the spread of the distribution around the mean.

Example 5-14: Bond Investment






Example 5-14

EX <- sum(X_x * P_x)

# Bond Y
X_y <- c(90, -30); P_y <- c(0.60, 0.40)
EY <- sum(X_y * P_y)

title: Statistics
text:
Binomial Experiments






Definition


A binomial experiment satisfies all four of the following conditions:

There is a fixed number of trials n.
Each trial has only two possible outcomes: success or failure.
The outcomes of each trial are independent of one another.
The probability of success p remains the same for every trial.




Examples: Tossing a coin n times; surveying n people with a yes/no question; testing n components with replacement.

title: Statistics
text:
Notation for the Binomial Distribution






Notation





Symbol
Meaning




P(S)
Probability of success


P(F)
Probability of failure


p
Numerical probability of success


q = 1 - p
Numerical probability of failure


n
Number of trials


X
Number of successes in n trials



Note: 0 \leq X \leq n and X = 0, 1, 2, \ldots, n

title: Statistics
text:
Binomial Probability Formula






Formula


In a binomial experiment, the probability of exactly X successes in n trials is:
P(X) = \frac{n!}{(n-X)!\,X!} \cdot p^X \cdot q^{n-X}
where q = 1 - p.




\dfrac{n!}{(n-X)!\,X!} = {}_nC_X counts the number of ways to arrange X successes among n trials
p^X is the probability of X successes
q^{n-X} is the probability of n - X failures

title: Statistics
text:
Example 5-15: Tossing Coins






Example 5-15


A coin is tossed 3 times. Find the probability of getting exactly 2 heads.




n <- 3; X <- 2; p <- 0.5; q <- 1 - p
prob <- choose(n, X) * p^X * q^(n - X)
cat("n =", n, ", X =", X, ", p =", p, ", q =", q, "\n")

n = 3 , X = 2 , p = 0.5 , q = 0.5 

cat("P(2 heads) = C(3,2) × (0.5)² × (0.5)¹ =",
    choose(n,X), "×", p^X, "×", q^(n-X), "=", prob)

P(2 heads) = C(3,2) × (0.5)² × (0.5)¹ = 3 × 0.25 × 0.5 = 0.375

# Verification using dbinom
cat("\nVerification via dbinom:", dbinom(2, size = 3, prob = 0.5))


Verification via dbinom: 0.375








Important


The coin-toss problem meets all 4 binomial conditions: fixed n=3 trials, two outcomes (H/T), independent tosses, constant p=0.5.

text:
Mean, Variance, and SD for the Binomial Distribution






Simplified Formulas for the Binomial Distribution


\mu = n \cdot p
\sigma^2 = n \cdot p \cdot q
\sigma = \sqrt{n \cdot p \cdot q}
These are algebraically equivalent to the general formulas \mu = \sum X \cdot P(X) and \sigma^2 = \sum[X^2 \cdot P(X)] - \mu^2.

title: Statistics
text:
Overview of Other Discrete Distributions
When the binomial model does not apply, other discrete distributions are available:



Distribution
When to Use




Multinomial
More than two outcomes per trial


Poisson
Events over time/area/volume; large n, small p


Hypergeometric
Sampling without replacement

title: Statistics
text:
The Multinomial Distribution






Formula


If an experiment has k possible outcomes E_1, E_2, \ldots, E_k with probabilities p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_k, and X_i is the number of times outcome E_i occurs in n independent trials, then:
P(X) = \frac{n!}{X_1!\, X_2!\, X_3!\, \cdots\, X_k!} \cdot p_1^{X_1} \cdot p_2^{X_2} \cdots p_k^{X_k}
where X_1 + X_2 + \cdots + X_k = n and p_1 + p_2 + \cdots + p_k = 1.



The multinomial distribution generalizes the binomial — the binomial is a special case with k = 2.

title: Statistics
text:
Example 5-24: Leisure Activities






Example 5-24


In a large city, 50% of residents choose a movie, 30% choose dinner and a play, and 20% choose shopping as a leisure activity. If 5 people are randomly selected, find the probability that 3 plan to see a movie, 1 to a play, and 1 to a shopping mall.




n <- 5
X1 <- 3; X2 <- 1; X3 <- 1   # movie, play, shopping
p1 <- 0.50; p2 <- 0.30; p3 <- 0.20

prob <- factorial(n) / (factorial(X1)*factorial(X2)*factorial(X3)) *
        p1^X1 * p2^X2 * p3^X3

cat("P(X) = 5!/(3!·1!·1!) × (0.50)³ × (0.30)¹ × (0.20)¹\n")

P(X) = 5!/(3!·1!·1!) × (0.50)³ × (0.30)¹ × (0.20)¹

cat("     =", factorial(n)/(factorial(X1)*factorial(X2)*factorial(X3)),
    "×", p1^X1, "×", p2^X2, "×", p3^X3, "\n")

     = 20 × 0.125 × 0.3 × 0.2 

cat("     =", round(prob, 4))

     = 0.15

        p1^X1 * p2^X2 * p3^X3 * p4^X4

title: Statistics
text:
The Poisson Distribution






Definition & Formula


The Poisson distribution applies when events occur randomly over a continuous interval of time, area, or volume — especially when n is large and p is small.
P(X;\, \lambda) = \frac{e^{-\lambda}\, \lambda^X}{X!}, \quad X = 0, 1, 2, \ldots

\lambda (lambda) = mean number of occurrences per unit interval
e \approx 2.71828 (Euler’s number)
X = number of occurrences in the interval

Also used to approximate the binomial when \lambda = n \cdot p < 5.

title: Statistics
text:
Example 5-27: Typographical Errors






Example 5-27


A 500-page manuscript contains 200 randomly distributed typographical errors. Find the probability that a given page contains exactly 3 errors.




lambda <- 200 / 500   # mean errors per page
X <- 3
prob <- (exp(-lambda) * lambda^X) / factorial(X)
cat("λ = 200/500 =", lambda, "errors per page\n")

λ = 200/500 = 0.4 errors per page

cat("P(X=3; λ=0.4) = e^(-0.4) × (0.4)³ / 3!\n")

P(X=3; λ=0.4) = e^(-0.4) × (0.4)³ / 3!

cat("              =", round(exp(-lambda), 6), "×", lambda^X, "/", factorial(X),
    "\n              =", round(prob, 4))

              = 0.67032 × 0.064 / 6 
              = 0.0072

# Verification
cat("\nVerification via dpois:", round(dpois(X, lambda), 4))


Verification via dpois: 0.0072

title: Statistics
text:
The Hypergeometric Distribution






Definition & Formula


The hypergeometric distribution applies when sampling is done without replacement from a finite population containing two types of objects.
Given a population with a items of type 1 and b items of type 2 (total a + b), the probability of selecting exactly X items of type 1 in a sample of size n is:
P(X) = \frac{C^a_X \cdot  C^b_{n-X}}{C^{a+b}_n}



Key difference from binomial: trials are dependent (no replacement).

title: Statistics
text:
Example 5-30: Assistant Manager Applicants






Example 5-30


Ten people apply for a restaurant assistant manager position: 5 are college graduates and 5 are not. If the manager selects 3 at random, find the probability that all 3 are college graduates.




a <- 5   # college graduates
b <- 5   # non-graduates
n <- 3   # sample size
X <- 3   # desired successes

prob <- choose(a, X) * choose(b, n - X) / choose(a + b, n)
cat("a =", a, "(graduates), b =", b, "(non-grads), n =", n, ", X =", X, "\n")

a = 5 (graduates), b = 5 (non-grads), n = 3 , X = 3 

cat("P(X) = C(5,3)×C(5,0) / C(10,3)\n")

P(X) = C(5,3)×C(5,0) / C(10,3)

cat("     =", choose(a,X), "×", choose(b, n-X), "/", choose(a+b, n),
    "=", round(prob, 4), "(= 1/12)")

     = 10 × 1 / 120 = 0.0833 (= 1/12)

Example 5-31


A study found that 2 out of 10 houses in a neighborhood have no insurance. If 5 houses are selected from 10, find the probability that exactly 1 is uninsured.




a <- 2   # uninsured
b <- 8   # insured
n <- 5; X <- 1

prob <- choose(a, X) * choose(b, n - X) / choose(a + b, n)
cat("a = 2 (uninsured), b = 8 (insured), n = 5, X = 1\n")

a = 2 (uninsured), b = 8 (insured), n = 5, X = 1

cat("P(X=1) = C(2,1)×C(8,4) / C(10,5)\n")

P(X=1) = C(2,1)×C(8,4) / C(10,5)

cat("       =", choose(a,X), "×", choose(b,n-X), "/", choose(a+b,n),
    "=", round(prob, 4), "(= 5/9)")

       = 2 × 70 / 252 = 0.5556 (= 5/9)

Summary of Discrete Distributions



Table 5-1: Summary of Discrete Distributions







Distribution
Formula
Use When




Binomial
P(X) = C^n_X·p^x·q^{n-x}
Fixed n trials; 2 outcomes; independent; constant p


Multinomial
P(X) = n!/(X_1!·X_2!···X_k!)·p_1^{X_1}···p_k^{X_k}

title: Statistics
text:
Chapter 5 Summary






Key Takeaways



A discrete probability distribution lists all possible values and their probabilities; requires \sum P(X)=1 and 0 \leq P(X) \leq 1.
Mean: \mu = \sum X \cdot P(X); Variance: \sigma^2 = \sum[X^2 \cdot P(X)] - \mu^2
Expected value E(X) = \mu — the long-run average outcome.
Binomial: n fixed trials, 2 outcomes, independent, constant p.

P(X) = C(n,X) \cdot p^X \cdot q^{n-X}; \mu = np; \sigma = \sqrt{npq}

Multinomial: extension of binomial for k > 2 outcomes.
Poisson: events over time/area; P(X;\lambda) = e^{-\lambda}\lambda^X / X!
Hypergeometric: two outcomes, sampling without replacement.

Chapter Overview
Sections covered:

6-1 Normal Distributions
6-2 Applications of the Normal Distribution
6-3 The Central Limit Theorem
6-4 The Normal Approximation to the Binomial Distribution

The normal distribution is the most important and widely used continuous probability distribution in statistics. Its familiar bell-shaped curve appears throughout natural phenomena, measurement errors, and statistical inference.

title: Statistics
text:
Properties of the Normal Distribution






Definition


A normal distribution is a continuous, symmetric, bell-shaped distribution of a variable. The curve is determined entirely by the mean μ and standard deviation σ.



Key properties:

The distribution is bell-shaped and symmetric about the mean
The mean, median, and mode are all equal
The curve is continuous — it never touches the x-axis
The total area under the curve equals 1
Approximately 68% of values lie within 1σ of μ; 95% within 2σ; 99.7% within 3σ

title: Statistics
text:
The Standard Normal Distribution






Definition


The standard normal distribution is a normal distribution with mean μ = 0 and standard deviation σ = 1. Values on this distribution are called z values or z scores.



The z score converts any normal variable X to the standard normal:
z = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma}

The z score represents the number of standard deviations X is from the mean
Area under the curve = probability

title: Statistics
section: Finding Areas Under the Standard Normal Curve
text:
Finding Areas Under the Standard Normal Curve
Areas are found using:

Table E (standard normal table) in textbook appendix
R: pnorm(z) gives P(Z < z)







Key R Functions



pnorm(z) — area to the left of z
1 - pnorm(z) — area to the right of z
pnorm(z2) - pnorm(z1) — area between z1 and z2
qnorm(p) — find z given left-tail area p

Find the following probabilities for the standard normal distribution:
(a) P(0 < Z < 2.32) (b) P(Z < 1.65) (c) P(Z > 1.91)




# (a) P(0 < Z < 2.32)

text:
Example 6-5: Finding a z Value Given an Area






Example 6-5


Find the z value such that the area to the left is 0.7123.



Solution (Mathematical):

Search Table E for the area closest to 0.7123
The corresponding z value is z = 0.56


# Find z given left-tail area = 0.7123
qnorm(0.7123)

[1] 0.5601165








Key Rule


qnorm(p) is the inverse of pnorm(z). Use it whenever you need the z value for a given probability.

title: Statistics
text:
Applying the Normal Distribution
To find probabilities for a non-standard normal variable X (with mean μ and standard deviation σ):






Formula


z = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma}
Convert X to a z score, then find the area using the standard normal.



In R, use pnorm(x, mean = μ, sd = σ) directly — no conversion needed.






Key Steps



Identify μ and σ
Draw a diagram and shade the desired region
Convert X to z (or use R directly)
Find the probability

text:
Example 6-6: Summer Spending






Example 6-6


The average amount of money that Americans spend on summer travel is normally distributed with μ = $146.21 and σ = $29.44. Find the probability that a randomly selected American spends less than $160 on summer travel.



Solution:
z = \frac{160 - 146.21}{29.44} = \frac{13.79}{29.44} \approx 0.47
Area to the left of z = 0.47 → 0.6808 (68.08%)

mu <- 146.21; sigma <- 29.44
pnorm(160, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

[1] 0.6802544

text:
Example 6-7: Newspaper Recycling






Example 6-7


Each month, an American household generates an average of 28 pounds of newspaper for recycling, with σ = 2 pounds. Assume a normal distribution.
(a) P(27 < X < 31) (b) P(X > 30.2)




mu <- 28; sigma <- 2

# (a) P(27 < X < 31)
pnorm(31, mu, sigma) - pnorm(27, mu, sigma)

[1] 0.6246553

# (b) P(X > 30.2)
pnorm(30.2, mu, sigma, lower.tail = FALSE)

[1] 0.1356661


Answers: (a) ≈ 62.47%; (b) ≈ 13.57%

title: Statistics
text:
Example 6-8: Coffee Consumption






Example 6-8


The per-capita consumption of coffee is normally distributed with μ = 1.64 gallons per year and σ = 0.24 gallons. In a sample of 500 people, how many consume less than 1 gallon per year?




mu <- 1.64; sigma <- 0.24

# Probability of consuming less than 1 gallon
p <- pnorm(1, mean = mu, sd = sigma)
p

[1] 0.003830381

# Expected number in sample of 500
round(p * 500)

[1] 2


Interpretation: Only about 0.4% of people drink less than 1 gallon — approximately 2 people in a sample of 500.

title: Statistics
text:
Example 6-9: Police Academy






Example 6-9


To qualify for a police academy, applicants are tested on their physical fitness. The scores are normally distributed with μ = 200 and σ = 20. The top 10% of applicants will be accepted. Find the minimum score needed.



Solution (Mathematical):

Need the 90th percentile → find z such that P(Z < z) = 0.90
z ≈ 1.28
X = μ + z·σ = 200 + 1.28(20) = 225.6 ≈ 226


mu <- 200; sigma <- 20
# Find the value X such that P(X > x) = 0.10
qnorm(0.90, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

[1] 225.631


Answer: An applicant needs a score of at least 226 to be in the top 10%.

title: Statistics
text:
Example 6-10: Blood Pressure






Example 6-10


For a certain group, systolic blood pressure is normally distributed with μ = 120 and σ = 8. Find the range of pressures that includes the middle 60% of readings.



Solution:

Middle 60% → 20% in each tail → find z for P(Z < z) = 0.20 and P(Z < z) = 0.80
z₁ ≈ −0.84, z₂ ≈ +0.84
X₁ = 120 + (−0.84)(8) = 113.28
X₂ = 120 + (0.84)(8) = 126.72


mu <- 120; sigma <- 8
# Lower and upper bounds for middle 60%
qnorm(0.20, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

[1] 113.267

qnorm(0.80, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

[1] 126.733


Answer: The middle 60% of readings fall between 113.28 and 126.72 mmHg.

title: Statistics
text:
Example 6-11: Technology Inventories






Example 6-11


A researcher claims that the distribution of technology inventories at warehouses is approximately normal with μ = 110,000 and σ = 15,000 units. A warehouse is selected at random. Find the probability that it has more than 132,500 units.




mu <- 110000; sigma <- 15000

# P(X > 132500)
pnorm(132500, mean = mu, sd = sigma, lower.tail = FALSE)

[1] 0.0668072

# Equivalent z-score
z <- (132500 - mu) / sigma
z

[1] 1.5

pnorm(z, lower.tail = FALSE)

[1] 0.0668072


Answer: z = 1.50, P(X > 132,500) ≈ 0.0668 (about 6.68%).

title: Statistics
text:
Example 6-12: Baseball Game Duration






Example 6-12


The distribution of the duration of professional baseball games is negatively skewed with μ = 166 minutes and σ = 26 minutes. If a game is selected at random, find the probability that it lasts less than 145 minutes.









Caution


This distribution is not normal — it is negatively skewed. Applying normal distribution methods is only appropriate when the distribution is approximately normal. Here the answer is an approximation.




mu <- 166; sigma <- 26
# Approximate probability (treating as normal)
z <- (145 - mu) / sigma
z

[1] -0.8076923

pnorm(145, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

[1] 0.2096339


Note: z ≈ −0.81; P(X < 145) ≈ 0.2090 (approximately 20.9%). Since the data is skewed, this is only a rough estimate.

title: Statistics
text:
The Central Limit Theorem






The Central Limit Theorem (CLT)


As sample size n increases, the sampling distribution of the sample mean \bar{X} approaches a normal distribution, regardless of the shape of the population distribution, provided n is sufficiently large (typically n ≥ 30).
\mu_{\bar{X}} = \mu \qquad \sigma_{\bar{X}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}



The standard error \sigma_{\bar{X}} = \sigma/\sqrt{n} measures how much sample means vary from sample to sample.

title: Statistics
text:
Applying the CLT






z Score for Sample Means


z = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}



In R: Use pnorm(xbar, mean = μ, sd = σ/sqrt(n))
The CLT explains why the normal distribution is so central to statistics:

Survey results, poll averages, sample statistics all tend toward normality
Enables inference even when the population shape is unknown

title: Statistics
text:
Example 6-13: Children’s TV Viewing






Example 6-13


Children in the United States watch an average of μ = 25 hours of TV per week, with σ = 3 hours. A random sample of n = 20 children is selected. Find the probability that the sample mean exceeds 26.3 hours.



Solution:
z = \frac{26.3 - 25}{3/\sqrt{20}} = \frac{1.3}{0.671} \approx 1.94
P(\bar{X} > 26.3) = P(Z > 1.94) ≈ 0.0262 (2.62%)

mu <- 25; sigma <- 3; n <- 20
se <- sigma / sqrt(n)
se

[1] 0.6708204

# P(X-bar > 26.3)
pnorm(26.3, mean = mu, sd = se, lower.tail = FALSE)

[1] 0.02631615

title: Statistics
text:
Example 6-14: Vehicle Age






Example 6-14


The average age of vehicles registered in the United States is μ = 96 months, with σ = 16 months. Assume the distribution is approximately normal. A random sample of n = 36 vehicles is taken. Find P(90 < \bar{X} < 100).




mu <- 96; sigma <- 16; n <- 36
se <- sigma / sqrt(n)
se

[1] 2.666667

# P(90 < X-bar < 100)
pnorm(100, mean = mu, sd = se) - pnorm(90, mean = mu, sd = se)

[1] 0.9209683


Answer: P(90 < \bar{X} < 100) ≈ 0.9211 (92.11%)
The sample mean is very likely to fall in this range because the standard error is only 2.67 months.

title: Statistics
text:
Example 6-15: Meat Consumption






Example 6-15


The average annual meat consumption per person is μ = 218.4 pounds, σ = 25 pounds.
(a) Find P(X < 224) for a single individual. (b) Find P(\bar{X} < 224) for a sample of n = 40 individuals.




mu <- 218.4; sigma <- 25; n <- 40

# (a) Individual: P(X < 224)
pnorm(224, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

[1] 0.5886213

# (b) Sample mean: P(X-bar < 224), n = 40
se <- sigma / sqrt(n)
pnorm(224, mean = mu, sd = se)

[1] 0.9217147


Answers: (a) ≈ 58.71%; (b) ≈ 92.22%






Key Insight


The probability is much higher for the sample mean because the standard error (σ/√n) is smaller than σ — sample means are less variable than individual values.

title: Statistics
text:
Why Use the Normal Approximation?
The binomial distribution is exact but computationally intensive for large n. The normal distribution provides a convenient approximation.






When to Use the Normal Approximation


Use the normal approximation to the binomial when: np \geq 5 \quad \text{and} \quad nq \geq 5 where q = 1 − p.
The approximating normal distribution has: \mu = np \qquad \sigma = \sqrt{npq}

title: Statistics
text:
Correction for Continuity






Correction for Continuity


Since we are approximating a discrete distribution with a continuous one, add or subtract 0.5 from X:



Binomial Expression
Normal Approximation




P(X = a)
P(a − 0.5 < X < a + 0.5)


P(X ≥ a)
P(X > a − 0.5)


P(X > a)
P(X > a + 0.5)


P(X ≤ a)
P(X < a + 0.5)


P(X < a)
P(X < a − 0.5)

text:
Example 6-17: Widowed Bowlers






Example 6-17


Researchers found that 10% of people who bowl are widowed. If 200 bowlers are selected, find the probability that 10 or more are widowed.



Check: np = 20 ≥ 5, nq = 180 ≥ 5 ✓
Parameters: μ = 20, σ = √(200 × 0.10 × 0.90) = √18

n <- 200; p <- 0.10; q <- 0.90
mu <- n * p; sigma <- sqrt(n * p * q)
cat("mu =", mu, "  sigma =", round(sigma, 4), "\n")

mu = 20   sigma = 4.2426 

# P(X >= 10) with continuity correction: P(X > 9.5)
pnorm(9.5, mean = mu, sd = sigma, lower.tail = FALSE)

[1] 0.9933358

# Exact binomial for comparison
pbinom(9, n, p, lower.tail = FALSE)

[1] 0.9964714


Answer: ≈ 0.9934 (99.34%) — it is extremely likely that 10 or more widowed bowlers appear in such a sample.

text:
Example 6-18: Batting Averages






Example 6-18


In baseball, a .320 batting average means a player gets a hit 32% of the time. In 100 at-bats, find the probability of getting 26 or fewer hits.



Check: np = 32 ≥ 5, nq = 68 ≥ 5 ✓
Parameters: μ = 32, σ = √(100 × 0.32 × 0.68)

mu = 32   sigma = 4.6648 

# P(X <= 26) with continuity correction: P(X < 26.5)

[1] 0.1191886

# Exact binomial
pbinom(26, n, p)

[1] 0.1180158


Answer (normal approx.): ≈ 0.119 (11.9%); Exact: ≈ 0.116.

title: Statistics
text:
Chapter Overview
Sections covered:

7-1 Confidence Intervals for the Mean When σ Is Known
7-2 Confidence Intervals for the Mean When σ Is Unknown
7-3 Confidence Intervals and Sample Size for Proportions
7-4 Confidence Intervals for Variances and Standard Deviations

title: Statistics
text:
Point Estimates vs. Interval Estimates






Point Estimate


A point estimate is a single numerical value used to estimate a population parameter. The best point estimate of the population mean μ is the sample mean \bar{X}.









Interval Estimate


An interval estimate is a range of values used to estimate a parameter. It acknowledges that the sample mean will differ from μ due to sampling variability.



A point estimate alone gives no sense of accuracy. An interval estimate — paired with a confidence level — tells us how reliable the estimate is.

title: Statistics
text:
Properties of a Good Estimator






Three Properties of a Good Estimator



Unbiased: The expected value of the estimator equals the true parameter
Consistent: As sample size grows, the estimator converges to the true value
Relatively Efficient: Among all unbiased estimators, it has the smallest variance




The sample mean \bar{X} satisfies all three properties — it is the preferred estimator of μ.

title: Statistics
text:
Confidence Level and Confidence Interval






Confidence Level


The confidence level is the probability that the interval estimate will contain the true population parameter, assuming the estimation process is repeated many times.









Confidence Interval


A confidence interval is a specific interval estimate of a parameter, determined from sample data and a chosen confidence level. Common levels: 90%, 95%, 99%.



Higher confidence → wider interval. There is always a trade-off between precision and certainty.

title: Statistics
section: Formula: Confidence Interval for μ (σ Known)
text:
Formula: Confidence Interval for μ (σ Known)






CI Formula (σ Known)


\bar{X} - z_{\alpha/2}\left(\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right) < \mu < \bar{X} + z_{\alpha/2}\left(\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right)



Confidence Level
z_{\alpha/2}




90%
1.65


95%
1.96


99%
2.58



The term E = z_{\alpha/2}(\sigma/\sqrt{n}) is the margin of error.



Assumptions:

Random sample;
n ≥ 30, OR population is normally distributed if n < 30.

title: Statistics
section: Example 7-1: Days It Takes to Sell an Aveo
text:
Example 7-1: Days It Takes to Sell an Aveo






Example 7-1


A researcher wants to estimate the average number of days it takes to sell a Chevrolet Aveo. A sample of 50 cars had a mean time of 54 days on the dealer’s lot. Assume the population standard deviation is 6.0 days. Find the best point estimate of the population mean and the 95% confidence interval.



Solution (Mathematical):
Point estimate: \bar{X} = 54 days
54 - 1.96\left(\frac{6.0}{\sqrt{50}}\right) < \mu < 54 + 1.96\left(\frac{6.0}{\sqrt{50}}\right) 54 - 1.7 < \mu < 54 + 1.7 \mathbf{52.3 < \mu < 55.7}

title: Statistics
section: Example 7-2: Waiting Times in Emergency Rooms
text:
Example 7-2: Waiting Times in Emergency Rooms






Example 7-2


A survey of 30 emergency room patients found an average waiting time of 174.3 minutes. The population standard deviation is known to be 46.5 minutes. Find the best point estimate and the 99% confidence interval of the true mean waiting time.



Solution (Mathematical):
174.3 - 2.58\left(\frac{46.5}{\sqrt{30}}\right) < \mu < 174.3 + 2.58\left(\frac{46.5}{\sqrt{30}}\right) 174.3 - 21.9 < \mu < 174.3 + 21.9 \mathbf{152.4 < \mu < 196.2} —

xbar <- 174.3; sigma <- 46.5; n <- 30; z <- 2.58
E <- z * sigma / sqrt(n)
cat("Point estimate:", xbar, "\n")

Point estimate: 174.3 

cat("99% CI: (", round(xbar - E, 1), ",", round(xbar + E, 1), ")\n")

99% CI: ( 152.4 , 196.2 )


Interpretation: We are 99% confident that the true mean ER waiting time is between 152.4 and 196.2 minutes.

title: Statistics
text:
Finding Other z_{\alpha/2} Values
For confidence levels other than 90%, 95%, or 99%, find z_{\alpha/2} as follows:

Convert the confidence level to a decimal: e.g., 98% → 0.98
Find \alpha = 1 - 0.98 = 0.02, so \alpha/2 = 0.01
The area in each tail is 0.01; look up 1 − 0.01 = 0.9900 in Table E
The corresponding z value is 2.33


# z_alpha/2 for common confidence levels
conf_levels <- c(0.90, 0.95, 0.98, 0.99)
z_vals <- qnorm(1 - (1 - conf_levels)/2)
data.frame(Confidence = paste0(conf_levels*100, "%"),
           z_alpha2 = round(z_vals, 3))

  Confidence z_alpha2
1        90%    1.645
2        95%    1.960
3        98%    2.326
4        99%    2.576

title: Statistics
text:
Example 7-3: Credit Union Assets






Example 7-3


The following data represent the assets (in millions of dollars) for a sample of 30 credit unions in southwestern Pennsylvania. Find the 90% confidence interval of the mean. Assume σ = 14.405.
12.23, 16.56, 4.39, 2.89, 1.24, 2.17, 13.19, 9.16, 1.42, 73.25, 1.91, 14.64, 11.59, 6.69, 1.06, 8.74, 3.17, 18.13, 7.92, 4.78, 16.85, 40.22, 2.42, 21.58, 5.01, 1.47, 12.24, 2.27, 12.77, 2.76




assets <- c(12.23, 16.56, 4.39, 2.89, 1.24, 2.17, 13.19, 9.16, 1.42,
            73.25, 1.91, 14.64, 11.59, 6.69, 1.06, 8.74, 3.17, 18.13,
            7.92, 4.78, 16.85, 40.22, 2.42, 21.58, 5.01, 1.47, 12.24,
            2.27, 12.77, 2.76)
xbar <- mean(assets); sigma <- 14.405; n <- length(assets)
z <- qnorm(0.95)   # 90% CI → alpha/2 = 0.05
E <- z * sigma / sqrt(n)
cat("X-bar =", round(xbar, 3), "\n")

X-bar = 11.091 

cat("90% CI: (", round(xbar - E, 3), ",", round(xbar + E, 3), ")\n")

90% CI: ( 6.765 , 15.417 )


Answer: 6.752 < \mu < 15.430 million. We are 90% confident that the mean assets of all credit unions in this region fall between $6.752M and $15.430M.

title: Statistics
text:
Sample Size for Estimating μ






Minimum Sample Size Formula


n = \left(\frac{z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sigma}{E}\right)^2
where E is the desired margin of error. Always round up to the next whole number.



What you need to know: - The desired confidence level (determines z_{\alpha/2}) - The population standard deviation σ (or an estimate from a prior study) - The acceptable margin of error E

title: Statistics
text:
Example 7-4: Depth of a River






Example 7-4


A scientist wants to estimate the average depth of a river. She wants to be 99% confident that the estimate is accurate within 2 feet. A previous study found σ = 4.33 feet. Find the minimum sample size needed.



Solution (Mathematical):
z_{\alpha/2} = 2.58, E = 2, \sigma = 4.33
n = \left(\frac{2.58 \times 4.33}{2}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{11.17}{2}\right)^2 = (5.585)^2 = 31.2 \rightarrow \mathbf{n = 32}

z <- 2.58; sigma <- 4.33; E <- 2
n_raw <- (z * sigma / E)^2
n_raw

[1] 31.20004

ceiling(n_raw)  # Always round UP

[1] 32


Answer: The scientist needs at least 32 measurements to achieve the desired precision with 99% confidence.

title: Statistics
text:
The t Distribution
When σ is unknown, the sample standard deviation s is used as a substitute. However, this introduces additional uncertainty — especially for small samples. The appropriate distribution is the Student’s t distribution.






Characteristics of the t Distribution


Similar to the normal distribution: 1. Bell-shaped and symmetric about the mean 2. Mean, median, and mode all equal 0 3. The curve never touches the x-axis
Differences from the normal: 1. Variance is greater than 1 (heavier tails) 2. It is a family of curves indexed by degrees of freedom (d.f.) 3. As d.f. increases, the t distribution approaches the standard normal

title: Statistics
section: Degrees of Freedom and the t Formula
text:
Degrees of Freedom and the t Formula






Degrees of Freedom


For a confidence interval for the mean: d.f. = n − 1
The degrees of freedom specify which t curve to use. In R: qt(p, df = n-1)









CI Formula (σ Unknown)


\bar{X} - t_{\alpha/2}\left(\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\right) < \mu < \bar{X} + t_{\alpha/2}\left(\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\right)
where t_{\alpha/2} is from Table F with d.f. = n − 1.



Assumptions: (1) Random sample; (2) n ≥ 30, OR population is approximately normally distributed if n < 30.

title: Statistics
section: When to Use z vs. t
text:
When to Use z vs. t






Decision Rule



σ is known → use z_{\alpha/2} with σ in the formula (any n, if normal or n ≥ 30)
σ is unknown → use t_{\alpha/2} with s in the formula (normal population or n ≥ 30)







When to Use z vs. t


Condition
Use




σ known, n ≥ 30
z and σ


σ known, n < 30 (normal pop.)
z and σ


σ unknown, n ≥ 30
t and s


σ unknown, n < 30 (normal pop.)
t and s

title: Statistics
text:
Example 7-5: Finding t_{\alpha/2}






Example 7-5


Find the t_{\alpha/2} value for a 95% confidence interval when the sample size is n = 22.



Solution (Mathematical):
d.f. = 22 − 1 = 21. Look up 95% column in Table F at row 21.
t_{\alpha/2} = 2.080

# t_alpha/2 for 95% CI with df = 21
qt(0.975, df = 21)   # upper tail area = alpha/2 = 0.025

[1] 2.079614








Key Rule


For a confidence interval, always use qt(1 - alpha/2, df = n-1). For a 95% CI: qt(0.975, df = n-1).

title: Statistics
text:
Example 7-6: Sleeping Time






Example 7-6


Ten randomly selected people reported their nightly sleep duration. The sample mean was 7.1 hours and the standard deviation was 0.78 hour. Find the 95% confidence interval of the mean. Assume the variable is normally distributed.



Solution (Mathematical):
σ unknown, n = 10 < 30 → use t distribution. d.f. = 9, t_{\alpha/2} = 2.262
7.1 - 2.262\left(\frac{0.78}{\sqrt{10}}\right) < \mu < 7.1 + 2.262\left(\frac{0.78}{\sqrt{10}}\right) 7.1 - 0.56 < \mu < 7.1 + 0.56 \mathbf{6.54 < \mu < 7.66}

text:

The data below represent the number of home fires started by candles each year over a 7-year period. Find the 99% confidence interval for the mean number of candle-caused home fires per year.

title: Statistics
text:
Proportions






Notation for Proportions


\hat{p} = \frac{X}{n} \quad \text{(sample proportion)} \qquad \hat{q} = \frac{n-X}{n} = 1 - \hat{p}
where X = number of units in the sample with the characteristic of interest, n = sample size.
The population proportion is denoted p (and q = 1 − p).



The sample proportion \hat{p} is an unbiased, consistent, and relatively efficient estimator of p. It also serves as the best point estimate of p.
Confidence interval formula: \hat{p} - z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}\hat{q}}{n}} < p < \hat{p} + z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}\hat{q}}{n}}
Condition: n\hat{p} \geq 5 and n\hat{q} \geq 5

title: Statistics
text:
Example 7-8: Air-Conditioned Households






Example 7-8


In a recent survey of 150 households, 54 had central air conditioning. Find \hat{p} and \hat{q}, where \hat{p} is the proportion of households with central air conditioning.



Solution (Mathematical):
\hat{p} = \frac{X}{n} = \frac{54}{150} = 0.36 = 36\% \hat{q} = \frac{n - X}{n} = \frac{150 - 54}{150} = \frac{96}{150} = 0.64 = 64\%

title: Statistics
text:
Example 7-9: Covering College Costs






Example 7-9


A survey of 1404 respondents found that 323 students paid for their education using student loans. Find the 90% confidence interval for the true proportion of students who fund their education through student loans.



Solution:
\hat{p} = 323/1404 = 0.230, \hat{q} = 0.770, z_{\alpha/2} = 1.65
0.230 \pm 1.65\sqrt{\frac{(0.230)(0.770)}{1404}} = 0.230 \pm 0.019 \mathbf{0.211 < p < 0.249}

title: Statistics
text:
Example 7-10: Religious Books






Example 7-10


A survey of 1721 people found that 15.9% purchase religious books at a Christian bookstore. Find the 95% confidence interval for the true proportion of people who purchase religious books there.



Solution:
\hat{p} = 0.159, \hat{q} = 0.841, z_{\alpha/2} = 1.96
0.159 \pm 1.96\sqrt{\frac{(0.159)(0.841)}{1721}} = 0.159 \pm 0.017 \mathbf{0.142 < p < 0.176}

p_hat <- 0.159; q_hat <- 1 - p_hat; n <- 1721
z <- 1.96
E <- z * sqrt(p_hat * q_hat / n)
cat("95% CI: (", round(p_hat - E, 3), ",", round(p_hat + E, 3), ")\n")

95% CI: ( 0.142 , 0.176 )


Answer: We are 95% confident the true percentage is between 14.2% and 17.6%.

title: Statistics
text:
Sample Size for a Proportion






Minimum Sample Size for a Proportion


n = \hat{p}\hat{q}\left(\frac{z_{\alpha/2}}{E}\right)^2

If a prior estimate of \hat{p} is available, use it
If no prior estimate is available, use \hat{p} = 0.5 (maximizes n, giving the most conservative estimate)

Always round up to the next whole number.

title: Statistics
text:
Example 7-11: Home Computers






Example 7-11


A researcher wishes to estimate with 95% confidence the proportion of people who own a home computer, to within 2% of the true proportion. A previous study showed that 40% had a computer at home. Find the minimum sample size needed.



Solution:
z_{\alpha/2} = 1.96, E = 0.02, \hat{p} = 0.40, \hat{q} = 0.60
n = (0.40)(0.60)\left(\frac{1.96}{0.02}\right)^2 = (0.24)(9604) = 2304.96 \rightarrow \mathbf{n = 2305}

p_hat <- 0.40; q_hat <- 0.60; z <- 1.96; E <- 0.02
n_raw <- p_hat * q_hat * (z / E)^2
n_raw

[1] 2304.96

ceiling(n_raw)

[1] 2305

title: Statistics
text:
Example 7-12: M&M Colors






Example 7-12


A researcher wishes to estimate the percentage of M&M’s that are brown. He wants to be 95% confident and accurate within 3% of the true proportion. No prior estimate of \hat{p} is available. Find the minimum sample size.



Solution:
Since no prior \hat{p} is known, use \hat{p} = \hat{q} = 0.5
n = (0.5)(0.5)\left(\frac{1.96}{0.03}\right)^2 = (0.25)(4268.4) = 1067.1 \rightarrow \mathbf{n = 1068}

title: Statistics
text:
The Chi-Square Distribution
Confidence intervals for variances and standard deviations require a different distribution — the chi-square (χ²) distribution.






Chi-Square Distribution Properties



Obtained from values of (n-1)s^2/\sigma^2 from normal populations
Cannot be negative; skewed to the right
A family of curves indexed by degrees of freedom (d.f. = n − 1)
Total area under each curve = 1
Approaches symmetry as d.f. increases (around 100+)

Key difference from z and t: The chi-square distribution is not symmetric, so two separate critical values (\chi^2_{\text{right}} and \chi^2_{\text{left}}) are needed.

title: Statistics
section: Formulas for Variance and Standard Deviation CIs
text:
Formulas for Variance and Standard Deviation CIs






Confidence Interval for a Variance


\frac{(n-1)s^2}{\chi^2_{\text{right}}} < \sigma^2 < \frac{(n-1)s^2}{\chi^2_{\text{left}}} d.f. = n − 1









Confidence Interval for a Standard Deviation


\sqrt{\frac{(n-1)s^2}{\chi^2_{\text{right}}}} < \sigma < \sqrt{\frac{(n-1)s^2}{\chi^2_{\text{left}}}}



Assumptions: (1) Random sample; (2) Population must be normally distributed.
Finding critical values: Use qchisq() in R. For a 95% CI with d.f. = n − 1: - \chi^2_{\text{right}}: qchisq(0.975, df = n-1) - \chi^2_{\text{left}}: qchisq(0.025, df = n-1)

title: Statistics
text:
Example 7-13: Finding Chi-Square Critical Values






Example 7-13


Find the values \chi^2_{\text{right}} and \chi^2_{\text{left}} for a 90% confidence interval when n = 25.



Solution (Mathematical):
d.f. = 25 − 1 = 24

\alpha = 1 - 0.90 = 0.10, so \alpha/2 = 0.05
\chi^2_{\text{right}}: area to right = 0.05 → column 0.05 → 36.415
\chi^2_{\text{left}}: area to right = 0.95 → column 0.95 → 13.848

title: Statistics
text:
Example 7-14: Nicotine Content






Example 7-14


Find the 95% confidence interval for the variance and standard deviation of the nicotine content of cigarettes manufactured, given that a sample of n = 20 cigarettes has a standard deviation of s = 1.6 milligrams.



Solution (Mathematical):
d.f. = 19; 95% CI → \chi^2_{\text{right}} = 32.852, \chi^2_{\text{left}} = 8.907
\frac{(19)(1.6)^2}{32.852} < \sigma^2 < \frac{(19)(1.6)^2}{8.907} \frac{48.64}{32.852} < \sigma^2 < \frac{48.64}{8.907} \implies \mathbf{1.5 < \sigma^2 < 5.5}
\sqrt{1.5} < \sigma < \sqrt{5.5} \implies \mathbf{1.2 < \sigma < 2.3}

title: Statistics
text:
Overview
Statistical hypothesis testing is a decision-making procedure used to evaluate a claim about a population parameter.






Key Vocabulary



Statistical hypothesis: A conjecture about a population parameter
Null hypothesis (H₀): States no difference or no effect — the status quo
Alternative hypothesis (H₁): The research claim; what we try to support
Test value: A computed statistic used to decide between H₀ and H₁

title: Statistics
text:
Chapter Sections

8-1 Steps in Hypothesis Testing — Traditional Method
8-2 z Test for a Mean
8-3 t Test for a Mean
8-4 z Test for a Proportion
8-5 χ² Test for a Variance or Standard Deviation
8-6 Additional Topics Regarding Hypothesis Testing

title: Statistics
text:
Null and Alternative Hypotheses






Hypothesis Structure



H₀ (null hypothesis): Contains equality (=, ≤, ≥)
H₁ (alternative/research hypothesis): Contains inequality (≠, <, >)
The claim may be in either H₀ or H₁




The direction of the alternative hypothesis determines the type of test:



H₁ contains
Test type




>
Right-tailed


<
Left-tailed


≠
Two-tailed

title: Statistics
text:
Types of Errors






Type I and Type II Errors





Decision
H₀ True
H₀ False




Reject H₀
Type I error (α)
Correct decision (1 − β)


Do not reject H₀
Correct decision (1 − α)
Type II error (β)




α = P(Type I error) = level of significance
β = P(Type II error)
Common values of α: 0.10, 0.05, 0.01

title: Statistics
text:
Critical Region and Critical Value






Key Terms



Critical (rejection) region: Range of values that lead to rejecting H₀
Noncritical region: Range of values that lead to not rejecting H₀
Critical value: Boundary separating the two regions

title: Statistics
text:
Example 8-1: Stating Hypotheses






Problem


State H₀ and H₁ for each claim:
(a) A researcher claims newborns weigh more than 8.6 lb on average.
(b) A manufacturer claims defective disks average fewer than 18 per 1000.
(c) A researcher claims background soft music changes exam scores from the mean of 73.



Solutions:
(a) Claim: μ > 8.6 → H₀: μ = 8.6 and H₁: μ > 8.6 (right-tailed)
(b) Claim: μ < 18 → H₀: μ = 18 and H₁: μ < 18 (left-tailed)
(c) Claim: μ ≠ 73 → H₀: μ = 73 and H₁: μ ≠ 73 (two-tailed)

title: Statistics
text:
Example 8-2: Finding Critical Values






Problem


Find the critical value(s) for each situation:
(a) Left-tailed, α = 0.10 (b) Two-tailed, α = 0.02 (c) Right-tailed, α = 0.005




# (a) Left-tailed, α = 0.10
qnorm(0.10)

[1] -1.281552

# (b) Two-tailed, α = 0.02 → α/2 = 0.01 on each side
qnorm(0.01)  # left; right is +2.326

[1] -2.326348

# (c) Right-tailed, α = 0.005
qnorm(1 - 0.005)

[1] 2.575829

title: Statistics
text:
Five-Step Hypothesis Testing Procedure






Traditional Method



State the hypotheses and identify the claim
Find the critical value(s) from the appropriate table
Compute the test value
Make the decision (reject or do not reject H₀)
Summarize the results in plain language

title: Statistics
section: The z Test for a Mean
text:
The z Test for a Mean






Formula


z = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma / \sqrt{n}}
Requirements: - Population standard deviation σ is known - If n < 30, the population must be approximately normally distributed



Use the standard normal (z) distribution to find critical values and P-values.

title: Statistics
text:
Example 8-3: Days on Dealers’ Lots (Traditional)






Problem


A researcher claims that cars sit on dealers’ lots more than 29 days on average. A random sample of 30 cars gives X̄ = 30.1 days; σ = 3.8. Use α = 0.05.



Step 1: H₀: μ = 29 and H₁: μ > 29 (claim; right-tailed)
Step 2: CV = +1.65
Step 3: Compute the test value.

xbar <- 30.1; mu <- 29; sigma <- 3.8; n <- 30
z <- (xbar - mu) / (sigma / sqrt(n))
round(z, 2)

[1] 1.59


Step 4: Since 1.59 < 1.65, do not reject H₀.
Step 5: There is not enough evidence to support the claim that cars sit more than 29 days.

title: Statistics
section: Example 8-4: Cost of Men’s Athletic Shoes (Traditional)
text:
Example 8-4: Cost of Men’s Athletic Shoes (Traditional)






Problem


A researcher claims the average price of men’s athletic shoes is less than $80. A sample of 36 shoes gives X̄ = $75, σ = $19.2. Use α = 0.10.



Step 1: H₀: μ = 80 and H₁: μ < 80 (claim; left-tailed)
Step 2: CV = −1.28

xbar <- 75; mu <- 80; sigma <- 19.2; n <- 36
z <- (xbar - mu) / (sigma / sqrt(n))
round(z, 2)

[1] -1.56


Step 4: Since −1.56 < −1.28 (falls in critical region), reject H₀.
Step 5: There is enough evidence to support the claim that the average price is less than $80.

title: Statistics
text:
Example 8-5: Rehabilitation Cost (Traditional)






Problem


A researcher claims the average rehabilitation cost for stroke patients differs from $24,672. A sample of 35 patients gives X̄ = $26,343, σ = $3251. Use α = 0.01.



Step 1: H₀: μ = 24672 and H₁: μ ≠ 24672 (claim; two-tailed)
Step 2: CV = ±2.58

xbar <- 26343; mu <- 24672; sigma <- 3251; n <- 35
z <- (xbar - mu) / (sigma / sqrt(n))
round(z, 2)

[1] 3.04


Step 4: Since 3.04 > 2.58 (falls in critical region), reject H₀.
Step 5: There is enough evidence to conclude that the rehabilitation cost differs from $24,672.

title: Statistics
text:
The P-Value Method






P-Value Decision Rule



Compute the P-value: the probability of obtaining a test statistic at least as extreme as the one computed, assuming H₀ is true
If P-value ≤ α → reject H₀
If P-value > α → do not reject H₀

Steps: 1. State hypotheses and identify claim 2. Compute the test value 3. Find the P-value 4. Make the decision 5. Summarize the results

title: Statistics
text:
Example 8-6: College Tuition (P-Value)






Problem


A researcher claims average tuition exceeds $5700. A sample of 36 schools gives X̄ = $5950, σ = $659. Use α = 0.05.



Step 1: H₀: μ = 5700 and H₁: μ > 5700 (claim; right-tailed)

xbar <- 5950; mu <- 5700; sigma <- 659; n <- 36
z <- (xbar - mu) / (sigma / sqrt(n))
round(z, 2)

[1] 2.28

# P-value for right-tailed test
p_val <- 1 - pnorm(z)
round(p_val, 4)

[1] 0.0114


Step 4: Since P = 0.0113 < α = 0.05, reject H₀.
Step 5: There is enough evidence to support the claim that average tuition exceeds $5700.

title: Statistics
text:
Example 8-7: Wind Speed (P-Value)






Problem


A researcher claims the average wind speed in a city is 8 mph. A sample of 32 days gives X̄ = 8.2 mph, σ = 0.6. Use α = 0.05.



Step 1: H₀: μ = 8 (claim) and H₁: μ ≠ 8 (two-tailed)

xbar <- 8.2; mu <- 8; sigma <- 0.6; n <- 32
z <- (xbar - mu) / (sigma / sqrt(n))
round(z, 2)

[1] 1.89

# Two-tailed P-value
p_val <- 2 * (1 - pnorm(abs(z)))
round(p_val, 4)

[1] 0.0593


Step 4: Since P = 0.0588 > α = 0.05, do not reject H₀.
Step 5: There is not enough evidence to reject the claim that the average wind speed is 8 mph.

title: Statistics
section: The t Test for a Mean
text:
The t Test for a Mean






Formula


t = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{s / \sqrt{n}}, \quad \text{d.f.} = n - 1
Use when: - σ is unknown (use sample s instead) - If n < 30, the population must be approximately normally distributed



Critical values come from the t distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom.

A hospital administrator claims the average number of infections per week is 16.3. A sample of 10 weeks gives X̄ = 17.7, s = 1.8. At α = 0.05, is there enough evidence to reject the claim?

Step 2: d.f. = 9; CV = ±2.262

xbar <- 17.7; mu <- 16.3; s <- 1.8; n <- 10
t <- (xbar - mu) / (s / sqrt(n))

qt(1 - 0.05/2, df = 9)  # critical value

text:
Example 8-16: Jogger’s Oxygen Uptake (P-Value)






Problem


A researcher claims that joggers’ maximum oxygen uptake exceeds 36.7 mL/kg/min. A sample of 15 joggers gives X̄ = 40.6, s = 6. Use α = 0.05.



Step 1: H₀: μ = 36.7 and H₁: μ > 36.7 (claim; right-tailed)

xbar <- 40.6; mu <- 36.7; s <- 6; n <- 15
t <- (xbar - mu) / (s / sqrt(n))

title: Statistics
section: The z Test for a Proportion
text:
The z Test for a Proportion






Formula


z = \frac{\hat{p} - p}{\sqrt{pq/n}}
where \hat{p} = X/n (sample proportion), p = hypothesized population proportion, q = 1 - p
Requirements: - Random sample - Binomial conditions satisfied - np ≥ 5 and nq ≥ 5

title: Statistics
text:
Example 8-17: Trans Fats (Traditional, Two-Tailed)






Problem


A dietitian claims 60% of people try to avoid trans fats. A survey of 200 people finds 128 trying to avoid them. At α = 0.05, is there enough evidence to reject the claim?



Step 1: H₀: p = 0.60 (claim) and H₁: p ≠ 0.60 (two-tailed)
Step 2: CV = ±1.96

X <- 128; n <- 200; p <- 0.60; q <- 1 - p
p_hat <- X / n
z <- (p_hat - p) / sqrt(p * q / n)
cat("p-hat:", p_hat, "  z:", round(z, 2))

p-hat: 0.64   z: 1.15


Step 4: Since 1.15 is between −1.96 and +1.96, do not reject H₀.
Step 5: There is not enough evidence to reject the claim that 60% of people try to avoid trans fats.
